sentences.text: Unlike its close relatives, this dinosaur possessed a much bulkier and more robust build.
The animal reached a total length of 11.6 meters and had a body mass ranging from 6 to 7.4 metric tons.
Its teeth were shaped like chisels, featuring wrinkled enamel surfaces, heavily serrated edges, and crowns that were flattened on the sides.
Scientists estimate the skull of this creature measured approximately 1.22 meters in length.
Unlike other known carcharodontosaurids, the sacral and caudal vertebrae of Tyrannotitan lacked pneumatic foramina extending into them.
The species possessed a fused and highly developed scapulocoracoid, yet it retained very small forelimbs.
The teeth were less lamellar than those of its relatives and featured unique denticle structures with a central groove dividing each denticle into two portions.
The proximal caudal vertebrae had an exceptionally high neural spine, approximately twice the size of the vertebral centrum.
Broken teeth found in the same rock layer as a giant sauropod suggest the animal broke its own teeth while tearing tough skin.
Tyrannotitan chubutensis was formally described by Fernando E. Novas, Silvina de Valais, Pat Vickers-Rich, and Tom Rich in the year 2005.
The only known species is represented by two fossil specimens that were found 400 meters apart by technicians Pablo Puerta and Leandro Guerrero.
These fossils were discovered at the La Juanita farm, located 28 kilometers northeast of Paso de Indios in Chubut Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
The diet primarily consisted of large herbivorous dinosaurs like Chubutisaurus and possibly juveniles or weaker sauropods like Patagotitan.
Evidence suggests the animal was an active hunter using a powerful bite, though it may have also scavenged opportunistically.
Fossil evidence suggests that Tyrannotitan persisted for millions of years after the death of the original two specimens found.
Tyrannotitan belongs to the tribe Giganotosaurini.
Canale et al. (2022) placed Tyrannotitan within the clade Giganotosaurini, alongside Meraxes, Giganotosaurus, and Mapusaurus.

The species shares specific anatomical traits with Mapusaurus and Giganotosaurus, including a wide postorbital process on the jugal, absence of pleurocoels in caudal vertebrae, and a reduced fourth trochanter on the femur.
Because Tyrannotitan skull remains are extremely incomplete, its head shape is reconstructed based on general family characteristics rather than direct evidence.
Tyrannotitan is classified as a member of the tribe Giganotosaurini.
Tyrannotitan lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.
The animal lived approximately 118 to 112 million years ago during the Aptian stage of the Middle Cretaceous in what is now South America.
Tyrannotitan lived during the Aptian stage, approximately 125 to 113 million years ago, in sediments of the Cerro Barcino Formation.
The Paleobiology Database records the time range of Tyrannotitan as the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 100.5 million years ago.
It is debated whether significant differences between Tyrannotitan and related taxa are due to evolution or sexual dimorphism, though the latter seems unlikely.
